intuition: Merge neighboring sorted sections of the list. Begin with sections of one node, which are already sorted. After merging, sections of two nodes are sorted; the next pass makes sections of four, then eight, and so on. This sorts by changing links rather than copying values into an array.

A one-node run is already sorted. Merge adjacent runs, doubling the guaranteed sorted width after each pass. split temporarily terminates each run so merge cannot wander into the next pair. A dummy node tracks the changing first node, while tail identifies the end of the output assembled during the current pass.
The final pair may contain a short run or no right run; the same merge logic handles it. Iteration avoids the recursion stack required by top-down merge sort.

At the start of a width pass, every width-sized run is sorted. Merging two adjacent sorted runs produces a sorted run of size at most 2*width and preserves its nodes. Thus each pass doubles the guaranteed sorted run size. Once width reaches n, the entire list is one sorted run. There are logarithmically many passes, each scanning O(n) nodes.
Only a fixed number of pointers is retained.

steps: Count four nodes in [4,2,1,3] and begin with width=1.
Cut [4] and [2]; merge their fronts into [2,4].
Cut [1] and [3]; merge them into [1,3], reconnecting both sorted runs.
Double width to 2 and merge [2,4] with [1,3] into [1,2,3,4].
Width becomes 4, so the complete list is one sorted run and dummy.next is returned.

concept.question: Can sorted one-node runs grow into a sorted whole chain?
intuition: Copying all values into an array and sorting would use linear extra memory. Recursive merging may also require call-stack memory. Bottom-up merging works directly with links.

One-node sections are already sorted. Merge neighboring sections of length one, then two, then four, doubling the known sorted run size after each full pass. Reconnect each merged run into the original chain.
concept.observation: At each pass, merge only neighboring sorted runs of the current size.
approach: Count nodes and begin with run size one.
Cut neighboring runs, merge their exposed minima, and reconnect them.
Double the run size until one sorted run spans the chain.
concept.correctness: Initially each size-one run is sorted. Merging two sorted neighboring runs by their exposed minima produces a sorted combined run containing exactly their nodes. A full pass therefore doubles the sorted run size. Once that size spans the node count, the entire chain is one sorted run, preserving every original node.

complexity.explanation: Every pass processes all nodes and the run size doubles, giving logarithmically many passes and overall linear-times-logarithmic work. Bottom-up link merging uses constant auxiliary memory.

pitfalls: Reconnect the output tail after every pair.
Do not claim constant memory for a copied array.
